summary: Defines the Session Description Protocol, a text format for describing multimedia sessions, used for announcing sessions, inviting people to them, and other kinds of session setup. It was replaced by RFC 4566.

eli5.summary: A card that says what a video call will use: who is calling, which sound and picture types, and where to send them.

questions: what does an sdp session description look like
what do the lines in sdp mean
what is the m= line in sdp
subtitle: A plain-text format that says what a multimedia session is, when it runs and how to join it.

tldr.problem: People joining a multicast conference needed a standard way to learn what the session is called, when it is active and which addresses, ports and media formats to use.
tldr.mechanism: SDP describes a session as lines of the form TYPE=VALUE in a fixed order, with a session-level part followed by one media-level part per stream. It is only a format and relies on other protocols such as SAP, SIP, RTSP, email or HTTP to carry it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2327 has been obsoleted by RFC 4566, and RFC 3266 updated it. It is not meant for negotiating media encodings.

today: RFC 2327 is obsoleted by RFC 4566, which is the current definition of SDP, and it was updated by RFC 3266. Its status is Proposed Standard.

sections.title: What SDP Is For
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes multimedia sessions for session announcement, session invitation and other forms of session initiation. It grew out of the session directory tools used on the Internet multicast backbone (Mbone) to advertise conferences.

To receive such a conference, a user mainly needs the multicast group address and the UDP ports of the data streams. SDP carries that information. It is purely a format: it has no transport protocol of its own and is meant to ride on others, including the Session Announcement Protocol (SAP), the Session Initiation Protocol, the Real-Time Streaming Protocol, email using MIME, and HTTP.

The RFC states that SDP is not intended for negotiating session content or media encodings.
sections.eli5: SDP is the card that says what the show is and where to tune in. It does not argue about which kind of TV to use.

sections.title: How Descriptions Travel
sections.content:
A common mode is for a client to announce a session by periodically multicasting a SAP packet to a well known multicast address and port. The SAP header is followed by a text payload holding the SDP description. That payload should be no greater than 1 Kbyte, and only one session announcement is permitted in a packet.

Descriptions can also be sent by email or on the web using the MIME content type application/sdp, which lets a mail reader or browser launch the right application. The catch is that a multicast session may be restricted in scope, so a person who gets the announcement by email or web may still be unable to receive the session. SAP announcements do not have that mismatch.
sections.eli5: You can pin the card to a notice board that everybody nearby sees, or mail it to a friend. A mailed card might point to a room the friend cannot reach.

sections.title: The Line Format
sections.content:
A description is entirely text, in ISO 10646 with UTF-8 encoding. Each line is <type>=<value>, where the type is exactly one case-significant character and no whitespace is allowed around the =. Text is used rather than a binary encoding for portability and so that many transports can carry it, but it is kept compact and has strict ordering rules so most errors produce malformed announcements that are easy to detect and discard.

A session-level part starts with v= and applies to the whole session. It is followed by zero or more media-level parts, each starting with m=. Session-level values are the defaults for all media unless a media-level value overrides them. Lines must appear in the order the RFC gives them, and optional lines are marked with an asterisk.

The set of type letters is deliberately small and not extensible: a parser must completely ignore an announcement that has a type letter it does not understand. Extension happens through a= attributes, and unknown attributes must be ignored.

Records end with CRLF, but parsers should also accept a single newline.
sections.eli5: Every line starts with a single letter and an equals sign, like a form with labelled boxes that always come in the same order. A reader that sees a box label it does not know throws the whole form away.

sections.title: The Fields
sections.content:
The required session-level lines are v= (protocol version, which is 0 with no minor number), o= (origin), s= (session name) and at least one t= (active time). The o= line holds a username, a session id, a version, a network type, an address type and an address. Together the username, session id and address identify the session, and the version rises when the description is modified. IN means Internet, and IP4 and IP6 are the address types.

Optional lines give an information string (i=), a URI (u=), email (e=) and phone (p=) contacts, and bandwidth (b=). Either an email or a phone line must be given. A c= connection line must be present at session level or in every media description. For multicast it carries a time to live, as in 224.2.1.1/127, and a third number can request several contiguous addresses.

Times in t= are NTP seconds. A stop time of zero means the session is unbounded, and zero for both means permanent. An r= line adds repeat times, for example every week. A z= line adjusts for daylight saving changes. A k= line can convey an encryption key by method clear, base64, uri or prompt.
sections.eli5: The card says who made it, what it is called, when it happens, who to call with questions, and which channel to tune in on. It can even say how often the show repeats.

sections.title: Media Descriptions and Attributes
sections.content:
Each media description starts with m=<media> <port> <transport> <fmt list>. Defined media types are audio, video, application, data and control. For UDP the port should be in the range 1024 to 65535, and for RTP it should be an even number, with the next odd port used for RTCP. The transports defined are RTP/AVP and udp. When several formats are listed, the first is the default.

For RTP, a static payload type such as 0 is fully defined by the audio/video profile. A dynamic type needs an a=rtpmap line, such as a=rtpmap:98 L16/16000/2, giving the encoding name, clock rate and optional parameters.

Attributes are the main extension point. They may be bare flags such as recvonly or name:value pairs. Suggested ones include cat, keywds, tool, ptime, sendrecv, sendonly, orient, type, charset, sdplang, lang, framerate, quality and fmtp. Unregistered attributes should begin with X-, and receivers ignore any attribute they do not understand.
sections.eli5: Each stream gets its own mini card saying whether it is sound or picture, which door number to use, and what kind of format it is in. Extra notes can be stuck on the card, and a reader just skips notes it cannot read.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A session description should not be trusted unless it was obtained over an authenticated transport from a trusted source. SAP offers encryption and authentication, but often the originator of an announcement cannot be authenticated because the receiver has never met them and no common public key infrastructure exists.

Because a description holds information used to start software, a parser MUST NOT be able to start anything except software specifically configured for multimedia sessions. It is normally inappropriate to start even that software without informing the user and getting their consent, so a description should not drop a user into an interactive session without their knowledge. This specification defines no attribute that starts tools in transmit mode.

Firewalls may parse descriptions to open holes for media. The RFC says it is inappropriate to open a hole for unicast streams unless the description came in a request from inside the firewall.
sections.eli5: Do not trust a card just because it showed up. A card should never be able to switch on your camera and microphone without asking you first.
